title: Making Decisions With Your Care Team
learningGoals: Understand shared decision making and informed consent
Ask about benefits, risks, alternatives, and timing for any recommendation
Tell the difference between decisions with time to talk and true emergencies
Make sure you understand, with plain words, an interpreter, or your support person
Know that you can ask for time, say not yet, or decline, and change your mind

slides.heading: Making Decisions With Your Care Team
onScreen: Module 4: Interventions and Flexible Decisions
slides.narration: Welcome to Module 4, Interventions and Flexible Decisions. Many births go as hoped, and some take a turn. Either way, you'll likely be part of some decisions along the way. In this first lesson, we'll talk about how those decisions are made with your care team, the questions that help, and what to do when time is short.

visual.description: A pregnant person and their support partner sitting with an ob-gyn in a calm exam room, all three leaning in over a printed page, talking.

slides.heading: You're part of the team
onScreen: Shared decision making: your team's knowledge plus your values
Informed consent: clear information, then your own choice
Your choice can include saying no
slides.narration: Good care is a partnership. Your care team brings medical knowledge and experience. You bring what matters most to you, your values, and your preferences. Shared decision making puts those together. Before most tests, treatments, or procedures, your team should explain what they recommend, why, and what the options are, in words you understand. Then the choice is yours. That's called informed consent, and it includes the right to say no.

visual.description: Two overlapping circles drawn as soft shapes: one holding a stethoscope, one holding a heart, with a small checkmark where they overlap. No words.

slides.heading: Four questions for any recommendation
onScreen: Why is this recommended for me?
What are the benefits and the risks?
What are the other options, including waiting?
How much time do we have to decide?
slides.narration: In Preparing for Birth, you learned the BRAIN questions. Here's a short version you can use for any recommendation, in pregnancy or in labor. Why is this recommended for me? What are the benefits, and what are the risks? What are the other options, including waiting? And how much time do we have to decide? That last question tells you a lot about what kind of decision you're facing.

visual.description: Four simple icons in a row: a question mark, a balance scale, two branching arrows, and a clock. No words.

slides.heading: How much time is there?
onScreen: Before labor: time to talk it over at visits, and to ask for a second opinion
In labor: often minutes to hours; you can ask for a few minutes to talk
An emergency: your team acts fast and explains as they go, or right after
slides.narration: Decisions come with different amounts of time. Before labor, there's usually time to talk things over at your visits, read more, and even get a second opinion. In labor, there's often time to ask your questions and take a few minutes alone with your support person before deciding. In a true emergency, your team may need to act quickly. They'll explain what they can as they go, and more afterward. It helps to talk about likely decisions ahead of time, so you're not hearing about them for the first time in labor.

visual.description: Three stacked bands from calm to urgent: before labor, in labor, and an emergency, each with how much time there usually is.

question.prompt: In labor, your nurse says the doctor recommends a change to your plan. You and your baby are doing well right now. What's a good first question?
options: There's nothing to ask; just agree
Why is this recommended, and how much time do we have to decide?
Can we decide after the baby is born?
question.explanation: Asking why and how much time there is helps you understand the recommendation and whether you can take a few minutes to talk it over.

slides.heading: Make sure you understand
onScreen: Ask for plain words, or a drawing
Say back what you heard: "So you're saying..."
Ask for an interpreter if you need one
It's okay to ask again
slides.narration: A choice only works if you understand it. If something isn't clear, ask your team to explain it in plain words, or to draw it. A good check is to say back what you heard: so you're saying, if we wait, this might happen. If you'd be more comfortable talking in another language, ask for a medical interpreter, rather than relying on a family member. And it's always okay to ask again, especially when you're tired or in pain.

visual.description: A doctor sketching a simple picture on a notepad for a pregnant person and their support person, who are nodding along. No readable writing on the notepad.

slides.heading: Your support person can help
onScreen: Ask questions when you can't
Write down what the team says
Remind everyone what matters most to you
slides.narration: Decisions are easier with someone beside you. Your support person can ask questions when you're in the middle of a contraction, write down what the team says, and remind everyone of what matters most to you. Talk with them before labor about your preferences, so they know your wishes. But the decision is still yours. Your support person helps you decide; they don't decide for you.

visual.description: A support partner sitting beside a laboring person in a hospital bed, holding a small notebook, while a nurse explains something at the bedside. No readable writing.

slides.heading: Saying "not yet" or "no"
onScreen: You can ask for more time, or say not yet
You can decline; your team will explain what may happen
Your decision will be written in your record
You can change your mind
slides.narration: You can ask for more time, say not yet, or decline a recommendation. If you do, your team should explain what might happen, and what they'd suggest instead, and they'll write your decision in your record. That's a normal part of care, not a sign of conflict. And you can change your mind later. Many families find that when they understand the reasons, they and their team end up agreeing on a plan.

visual.description: A pregnant person in a hospital gown talking calmly with a doctor and nurse at the bedside, everyone relaxed and listening.

slides.heading: A decision in labor
onScreen: Notice the questions they ask, and the pause they take
slides.narration: Here's a short example of a family making a decision with their care team during labor.

video.brief: In a calm labor room, a doctor explains a recommended change to the plan. The laboring person and their support partner ask why, what the options are, and how much time they have. The doctor says there's time to talk. The doctor and nurse step out for a few minutes; the couple talk quietly, then call the team back and share their decision, and everyone nods. Narration-free with soft music and short captions. No medical procedures shown.

slides.heading: What matters most to you
onScreen: The two or three things that matter most to you in labor
Who will help you decide
A question you want to ask your team before labor
slides.narration: Let's put this into practice. What are the two or three things that matter most to you in labor? Who will be with you to help you decide? And what's one question you want to ask your care team before labor starts, about a decision you might face? Save your answers to your Birth Readiness Brief, and bring them to your next visit.
slides.prompt: Write the two or three things that matter most to you in labor, who will help you decide, and one question for your care team.

slides.heading: What we covered
onScreen: Decisions are shared: your team's knowledge plus your values
Ask why, benefits and risks, other options, and how much time
Plain words, an interpreter, and your support person help
You can ask for time, say not yet, or decline
slides.narration: Let's recap. Decisions in pregnancy and birth are shared, combining your team's knowledge with your values. For any recommendation, ask why, what the benefits and risks are, what the other options are, and how much time there is. Ask for plain words or an interpreter, and lean on your support person. And remember, you can ask for time, say not yet, or decline. Next up, a few review questions.

options: Signing forms when you arrive at the hospital
Getting clear information about a recommendation, then making your own choice
Letting your support person decide for you
reviewQuiz.explanation: Informed consent means your team explains what they recommend, why, and the options, in words you understand, and then you choose, which can include saying no.

reviewQuiz.prompt: Which question best tells you whether you have time to talk a decision over?
options: Who else has had this done?
How much time do we have to decide?
reviewQuiz.explanation: Asking how much time there is tells you whether you can take a few minutes, or whether it's an emergency where your team needs to act quickly.

reviewQuiz.prompt: You'd rather talk about a medical decision in Spanish. What's the best step?
reviewQuiz.explanation: A medical interpreter helps make sure you understand your options and your team understands you.
